summary: Argues against proposals to mandate a special top-level domain name or an IP address bit to flag adult or unsafe material. It explains why this would be an ill-considered idea from legal, philosophical and especially technical points of view. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: Some people want one special label on the Internet that marks grown-up websites. This paper explains why that would not work well and would cause many problems.

questions: why not a .sex top level domain
can the internet flag adult content with an address bit
why not a .sex domain for adult content
should ip addresses flag content types
subtitle: Why a special domain for adult content would not work

tldr.problem: Periodically, politicians and commentators propose creating a special top-level domain (like .sex or .xxx) or reserving IP address bits to flag adult content and make it easier to block.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC examines why this idea fails from legal, philosophical, and technical perspectives: no global consensus exists on what is adult content, implementation is technically infeasible, and it creates free speech and privacy risks.
tldr.outcome: The RFC concludes that mandatory labeling at the domain or IP level is impossible, but suggests PICS (Platform for Internet Content Selection) as a decentralized alternative where multiple independent raters assign labels that users can choose to consult.

today: RFC 3675 remains relevant to discussions about Internet content filtering and governance. Proposals for special-purpose domains or IP bits continue to resurface periodically, and the RFC's technical and philosophical arguments remain applicable. The document has not been obsoleted.

sections.title: The Proposal and Its Problems
sections.content:
RFC 3675 examines a recurring policy proposal: creating a special top-level domain name (such as .sex, .xxx, or .adult) where all adult content would be required to reside, or alternatively, reserving an IP address bit or range to mark adult material. The proposal is motivated by the desire to make it easier for parents, schools, and others to block access to adult content.

The RFC demonstrates that this idea is fundamentally flawed from legal, philosophical, and especially technical standpoints. Rather than achieving the goal of content filtering, such a system would create new problems: it would be technically infeasible to implement, it would threaten free speech and privacy, and it would fail because the fundamental assumptions behind the proposal—that a global consensus on what is adult content could exist—are incorrect.
sections.plainLanguage: Governments and organizations keep proposing that all adult websites should use a special address or label. This paper explains why that would not actually work.

sections.title: Historical Context of the Proposals
sections.content:
The idea of a .sex or .xxx domain has been discussed for decades. In 1998, the U.S. House Commerce Committee said there were no technical barriers to creating an adult domain and that it would be easy to block all such sites. The British Telecom company supported the idea, and industry executives initially endorsed it. However, later industry participants preferred to continue using .com while optionally adding an adult domain, rather than switching entirely.

In 2000, the U.S. Congress's Commission on Child Online Protection explored both a .xxx domain and a .kids domain, concluding that while technically possible, they would be only moderately effective and raised privacy and free speech concerns. ICANN rejected .xxx in its initial round. More recently, Congress created a kids.us domain after determining that a global .kids domain was inappropriate. The debate shows a pattern of proposals being made, studied, and rejected due to fundamental problems.
sections.plainLanguage: Politicians and companies have been discussing this idea since the 1990s. Different groups studied it and realized it would not work well.

sections.title: Legal and Philosophical Concerns
sections.content:
The most fundamental problem is that every person, court, and government has different views on what sexual material is acceptable. The U.S. itself has no universal definition of obscenity; legal standards are based on community norms, which vary by location and over time. Across the world's over 200 countries and countless subdivisions, agreement on what belongs in an adult domain is impossible. A photographer conducting a legal shoot in Scandinavia could be prosecuted in the United States. The Netherlands and Saudi Arabia would never agree on categorization.

Creating such a domain would create an irresistible temptation for conservative legislators to force controversial publishers into it and prosecute those who remain in .com. The American Civil Liberties Union and other groups worry that publishers of health information about birth control, AIDS prevention, or gay and lesbian issues could be coerced into the adult domain and then blocked. Additionally, the domain could make it easier for repressive governments to monitor and prosecute users who visit such sites, and it could support arguments for future legislation that restricts free speech on the Internet.
sections.plainLanguage: Different countries and religions disagree strongly about what is acceptable. Forcing material into one category would cause legal fights and would let governments censor information unfairly.

sections.title: Technical Problems with Domain Names
sections.content:
From a technical standpoint, domain name labeling faces several insurmountable problems. First, the Domain Name System (DNS) relies on hierarchical delegation, where each zone is managed independently. If a website mixes material across categories, it would need separate domain names for each category (such as kids.example.com, adult.example.com, etc.), all in different DNS zones under different delegations. This quickly becomes unmanageable; for realistic categorization requiring hundreds of bits of information, you would theoretically need trillions of domain names.

Second, a domain's controller cannot prevent others from creating names that point to their IP address. Someone could create innocent.example.sex pointing to a legitimate website's IP address, or vice versa, completely defeating the labeling scheme. Third, protocols vary in how they use domain names: modern HTTP 1.1 servers can distinguish virtual hosts by domain name, but older systems, email forwarding, redirects, newsgroups, and IRC channels either do not use domain names hierarchically or lack central control. No single naming scheme can cover all these protocols consistently.
sections.plainLanguage: Websites have all types of material mixed together, so you would need hundreds of different domain names per site. Also, someone can trick the system by pointing any name to any website.

sections.title: Technical Problems with IP Addressing
sections.content:
Using IP address bits or ranges for content flagging is even more problematic. IP addresses are fundamentally tied to network routing and topology, not content. Routers use the most specific prefix match of the destination address bits to determine where to forward packets. Allocating any high-order bits for content labeling would either double the number of routing table entries (making routers too expensive) or require world-wide reconfiguration that is impossible to enforce.

IPv4 addresses are already in short supply, and reallocating even one bit for labeling would cut available addresses in half. Existing allocations have not been made with this in mind, so renumbering every organization on the Internet would cost billions of dollars. IPv6 provides more address space, but allocating 20 bits for realistic labeling would multiply routing table sizes by a million, far exceeding technical feasibility.
sections.plainLanguage: Internet addresses are used for routing data, not for labeling content. Using them for labeling would break the routing system or require impossible changes to every network.

sections.title: Alternative Approaches
sections.content:
Rather than mandatory, centralized labeling, the RFC points to PICS (Platform for Internet Content Selection) as a reasonable alternative. PICS allows multiple independent rating services to assign labels to content, and users select which raters to trust. A rater could provide labels for a particular community's standards, and different communities can have different raters. The system supports hundreds of dimensions of ratings (violence, language, sexual content, etc.) and does not require any single global consensus.

PICS labels can be digitally signed for authenticity and can be embedded in HTML, provided with HTTP responses, or obtained from third parties. This decentralized, opt-in approach respects the diversity of the world while still providing filtering options to those who want them. It avoids forcing speech, does not require protocol changes, and does not depend on global agreement on categories or on controlling the network's naming and addressing infrastructure.
sections.plainLanguage: A better approach is to let many different groups rate websites according to their own values, and let people choose which groups' ratings they trust.
